messages.content: Write a post about what a software company learned from a year of remote work. Around 250 words.

output:
**A year without an office**

We closed the office in March. Here's what actually changed.

Meetings got worse before they got better. In the office you could tell a conversation was over because people started looking at the door. On video nobody looks at anything, so we ran 45 minutes on things that deserved 10. We fixed it by defaulting every recurring meeting to 25 minutes and killing the ones nobody could write an agenda for. Eleven of nineteen died that way.

Writing became the job. Our design docs used to be three bullets and a photo of a whiteboard. Now they run two pages, and review comments went from "lgtm" to something you can argue with. That's the part I'd keep even if everyone came back tomorrow.

Onboarding broke. New hires shipped their first change in four days before the move, and in about three weeks after. Nobody was overhearing anything. We ended up giving each new person a named buddy with an hour a day blocked off, which is expensive and which worked.

The thing nobody warned us about: people stopped disagreeing. Disagreement needs a low-stakes channel, and Slack isn't one, because every objection looks permanent and quotable. Our best arguments used to happen at the coffee machine. We never replaced it. We tried a few things. None stuck.

Would we go back? No. But "remote works fine" is too smug an answer. It works if you're willing to rebuild the parts of the office you never noticed you were using.

---
